**Playbook for the sonar picket game.**

- The escort pool is the real money: mutual escort naming pays 5 each, more than a hit. From round 1 I should be working to set up a standing mutual escort deal with a specific boat and name them every round. I do this in my notes: post a note like "Echo will escort Foxtrot every round if Foxtrot escorts Echo." Then actually follow through on my escort claim every round. Sitting out with [salvage: none] earned nothing — never do that again unless defection is clearly better.

- Never fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll is tempting but the office puts me off the board for the rest of the patrol, which forfeits all future hits and escort payments. That trade is bad unless I'm already hopelessly behind in the final round, and even then escort money is safer.

- Fire at whoever the standing order names. Deviating breaks pattern with no payoff — the fire order is enforced socially and my shots hit or miss independent of compliance.

- Claims must match the private truth; they're validated. Lying (claiming a hit on a miss) gained me nothing — opponents don't seem to act on my public claims, and credibility is worth more if notes ever become informative. Always report truthfully.

- Hiding: no one demonstrated any ability to track my cell — misses were essentially random. So randomizing my hide cell is fine, but vary it; don't cluster near the middle (middle cells are the natural guess). If I'm the standing-order target of a live shooter, pick edge cells (1, 2, 8, 9).

- Firing: my target's hide cell is unknown and my guesses never improved on chance. Just pick a fresh cell each round — avoid cells I already missed at that target — and lean toward edges since players hide mid-line by default.

- Notes: short, coordinated, and used to build the escort deal, not filler. "Steady on station" bought nothing. Every note should either propose/confirm an escort pairing or share something actionable.

- Read the score at each round: if I'm behind late, the only catch-up levers are hits (4 points) and a sealed escort pair (5 points). Lock in the escort pair before the last round; on the final round there's no reason to defect from a pair.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK

**Escort claims are the main money.** A mutual escort pair pays 5 points each, more than a hit (4). In my run I never once named an escort partner and scored zero. From now on: every round, name the boat I think will name me back. Coordinate this through notes — a station note like "Foxtrot escorting Echo this round" is public and makes mutual claiming near-certain. Rotate partners across rounds to keep everyone willing.

**Standing order shooting is fine, but hitting matters less than escort payouts.** Fire at my assigned target as ordered (keeps me within the rules and predictable), but don't spend mental effort optimizing shot cells; spend it on the escort coordination.

**Claims must match the private result — no choice there.** Always report truthfully; there's no upside since the office already knows and the claim is forced to match. Don't waste a bluff idea here.

**Hiding: avoid repeating cells and avoid the middle.** I hid at 7 twice and got hit. When being fired on, pick different offbeat cells each round (1, 3, 7, 9 rotating), never center, and never reuse a cell that was hit or that I publicly hinted at.

**Notes should do work, not be noise.** "Steady on station" told Harbor and the others nothing and helped nobody. Use notes to propose escort pairings and to obscure my position with plausible-but-false location hints (e.g., "holding east of center" while hiding west).

**Never fire on Harbor.** The 3-point payroll is tempting, but the standing signal says I'm removed for the rest of the patrol — that threat makes it strictly bad unless the rules text shows no real enforcement.

**Final round:** keep claiming escorts even on the last round — the 5 points still count. Don't switch to "nothing to lose" plays like false claims; the claim is validated anyway.

**General shape of my play:** points come from (a) mutual escort deals, (b) landing shots on my assigned target, (c) not getting hit. Prioritize (a) — it's the only one fully under my control through communication.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK

- Fire stage: I always follow the standing order (fire at the next station in the cycle). Deviating to fire on Harbor looks tempting for the 3-point jettison, but Harbor's threat is explicit and the standing order produced zero retaliation all game. Keep to the cycle unless the scoreboard shows the order has broken down.
- Fire cell choice barely matters if others hide unpredictably; I'll just spread my shots across cells rather than repeating one number, since repeated cells all missed.
- Claim stage: I must report the true result — the claim is forced to match the private truth anyway. In the last round I claimed "hit" on a known miss and it gained me nothing. Never bluff here; it's just noise.
- Escort stage: this is where I bled points. Mutual escort claims pay 5 each, every round, and I claimed "none" every round out of caution. Next time I name one of the other boats each round and try to make it reciprocal: I pick the boat most likely to name me back (usually whoever isn't shooting at me this round or has been coordinating in notes). Even an unmatched claim costs nothing, so always name someone — "none" is strictly dominated. Echo and I were both shooting at each other's targets on schedule; pairing with Echo was free money I left on the table for six rounds.
- Hide stage: edge cells over the middle. If a particular opponent has hit me repeatedly, switch to an untried cell rather than clustering near previous spots; once I moved, I stopped being hit.
- Notes: keep them plain "steady on station" — they carry no information cost and no one used them for coordination. Don't waste effort signaling through them unless someone else starts using them to arrange escort pairs; if they do, I mirror their offer immediately.
- Priority of point sources: escort pairs (5/round, guaranteed if mutual) are far larger and more reliable than hit shots (4, random). Most of my attention goes to securing the escort pair every round; hiding and shooting are low-effort by comparison.
